Sepkoski Database Analysis

“No recent” = extinct genera only; “With recent” also includes genera still living today. Sepkoski Database of — fossil genera. M. Tikhonov et al. bioRxiv, 2026-07.

1Basic data

The record itself. The button above the panel steps through the five views; it is part of the page, never of a downloaded PNG.

2Luck versus toughness

Genera vs time: standing diversity through the whole record, data drawn solid and the model at the current luck dashed — blue for all living genera, red for those the small events are about to take. Slide luck until the red pair sits on top of each other.

Event Survival Curves: of those genera that reach to just before an event, the fraction that survive it, as a function of how long they had already existed.

Fractional Survival of genera alive at time t: of those genera, the fraction that exist just after an event.

Survivorship (Raup 1978, cohort analysis): subsequent survival probability of the genera that appear in one epoch, following the fraction still alive after each later extinction event; the bar marks the epoch the cohort was born into.

Survivorship traceback

Click a cohort bar or a sphere to add or drop a single event. The button above the lower panel steps between the four comparisons of model and data: genera vs time, event survival curves, fractional survival and survivorship.

Technical analysis
Realizations10
ε0.050

Sweeps the luck factor 0–2.5 (step 0.1) and scores each value with the full-curve RMS fit error of ref. 1 (Methods C): event survival curves on the epoch-boundary grid, cohorts under 10 genera masked out, model value = median over realizations, residuals standardised by the Jeffreys binomial error added in quadrature to ε. Solid = event survival curves, dashed = fractional survival, dotted = Raup cohort survivorship. Ochre is the overall fit over all events and is always shown; the in-panel button adds a fit restricted to the events before 250 Mybp (red) or after 250 Mybp (blue). Changing ε is instant; more realizations are smoother but slower.

The MSD panel is the mean-square model–data gap of the three measures, averaged over many events; its in-panel button cycles between them. Below the fit-error sweep sit the three lifetime distributions: genus lifetimes, order mean lifetimes, and lifetimes normalised by each order's mean.

3Extinction–Origination

The Origination–Extinction matrix counts the genera that originate at one boundary and disappear at another — the data panel above, the model at the same luck below. Read along a row and you have one of Raup's survivorship curves; read down a column and you have the age structure of one extinction.

4Taxonomic Orders

Order diversity through time and the two 3D maps. Tap a cylinder in either map for its order or class. (The lifetime distributions have moved to Technical analysis in section 2.)

The Data/Model switch in the corner of each 3D map matters here. The model kills the right number of genera at every event but not the right ones, so it knows nothing of taxonomy: under Model, groups no longer die out as units and most classes run to the present. Trilobites end at the Permian in the data and survive it in the model — that gap is the point, not a fault.

Silhouettes · what each drawing shows

Tap a cylinder in either 3D map and a small drawing of a representative member of that class appears under the info card. Every silhouette here was drawn for this applet as vector paths — original line art, nothing traced, photographed or copied, so there is no image licence to honour and nothing is fetched from the network. They are schematic and not to scale; the italic name is the genus the drawing is based on.

About this applet · abstract & references

In the fossil record it is the old who survive. A genus that has already weathered many an extinction is the more likely to weather the next, while the young perish easily. Must we then suppose that lineages grow hardier as they age? Using the Sepkoski marine genus compendium, this applet follows ref. 1 and asks the question the other way about: what if nothing in a genus ever changes, and the old merely appear sturdy because the frail were long ago swept away? That single idea — survivorship bias — with a single fitted parameter, reproduces the whole set of age-conditioned survival probabilities, the way extinction risk falls with genus age, and the distribution of genus lifetimes. The verdict is that Luck weighs a little heavier than intrinsic properties in the game of species survival. And Luck is here no idle word: it carries the fact that no two catastrophes are alike — one may be the ecosystem stumbling over its own feet (ref. 5), another the work of volcanoes, or of a stone that fell out of the sky.

The applet also lets the story be told a little differently, by giving every genus in a taxonomic order the same intrinsic toughness — as though fortune were dealt out by family rather than by individual. That toughness may be drawn at random; or it may be set in proportion to the average lifetime of the genera within the order, which is the more careful telling, for it lets kin meet the stresses of history together, as in truth they did. Fitted in that manner Luck grows more modest than intrinsic toughness: the best fit falls to 0.9, where before it stood at 1.5.

The applet opens the door to the orders themselves, to their diversity and their robustness (ref. 4). Among these views stands the Origination–Extinction matrix, which is, by its very construction, the whole family of Raup's (1978) survivorship curves gathered into a single picture — the same curves that were integrated along the extinction times in each of the survivorship curves of the analyses above.

Finally the applet opens for analyzing taxonomic classes in terms of the orders that they consist of, giving a bird's eye view on evolutionary relationships.

References

  1. M. Tikhonov, K. Sneppen, S. Bornholdt, & S. Maslov (2026). Survivorship Bias Explains Age-Dependent Extinction in Fossil Genera. bioRxiv, 2026-07.
  2. Sepkoski Jr, John J. “A compendium of fossil marine animal genera.” Bulletins of American Paleontology 363 (2002): 1–560.
  3. Raup, David M. “Cohort analysis of generic survivorship.” Paleobiology 4.1 (1978): 1–15.
  4. S. Bornholdt, K. Sneppen, & H. Westphal (2009). Longevity of orders is related to the longevity of their constituent genera rather than genus richness. Theory in Biosciences, 128(2), 75–83.
  5. P. Bak & K. Sneppen. “Punctuated equilibrium and criticality in a simple model of evolution.” Physical Review Letters 71.24 (1993): 4083.
  6. R. V. Solé & S. C. Manrubia. “Extinction and self-organized criticality in a model of large-scale evolution.” Physical Review E 54.1 (1996): R42.
  7. M. E. J. Newman. “A model of mass extinction.” Journal of Theoretical Biology 189.3 (1997): 235–252.
